extracted.intended_audience: Tabletop RPG Game Masters and worldbuilders running TTRPG campaigns
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice for Game Masters on designing and running magic systems in tabletop RPGs using Brandon Sanderson's laws—covering consistency, costs/limits/flaws, focusing design, and prioritizing fun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's First Law (Consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: “An author’s ability to solve conflict with magic in a satisfying way is directly proportional to how well the reader understands said magic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make how and why magic is used clear to players so magical solutions feel satisfying. Provide a coherent, consistent world; any feat of magic should adhere to rules as understood by players. Avoid deus-ex-machina or ad-hoc rule changes that feel unfair and pull players out of the game. Example anti-pattern: telling players 'it doesn’t work' when a counterspell is rolled; preferable is an in-world justification (e.g., the villain uses their own counterspell) so the outcome is consistent with established mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal logic of your story fits and is consistent with itself—no event or action within the narrative should contradict another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure game events, NPC behavior, and magic use follow the system's established internal rules. Players will notice deliberate violations; perceived DM tampering undermines immersion. Use established mechanics to resolve unexpected player actions rather than inventing exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: External consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify why things happen in your story to a person who understands the laws of our universe (leverage shared real-world understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground fantastic concepts with parallels to real-world logic when helpful (example: X‑men powers explained via an 'X‑gene'). External consistency helps players accept and understand fantastical elements. Use familiar analogies to explain mechanics when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's Second Law (Costs, Limitations, Flaws)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The costs, limitations, and flaws described in your story are what make your magic interesting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the narrative potential of restrictions rather than just powers. Explicitly define what paying a price, what unavoidable constraints exist, and what problems can be solved or improved—these drive dramatic tension and player choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost (deliberate penalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cost is a penalty for using magic. The costs are known by the magic users and willfully paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use costs to create trade-offs and meaningful decisions (example: the One Power causes rot/madness; Call of Cthulhu's Sanity loss). Make costs significant and difficult to trivially bypass so choices matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation (unchangeable constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation is a penalty that can’t be changed or avoided, and must simply be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use immutable limits as narrative equalizers (example: Kryptonite strips Superman’s powers; a wizard’s spell slots). Limitations force different tactics and create stakes when resources are exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flaw (fixable deficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: A flaw is a deficiency that can be fixed or changed; it provides a clear problem for the narrative to solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce flaws to give the campaign direction—quests to remove curses or restore lost powers (example: Elantris’s magic stops working; a cursed bard suffers harm when lying). Flaws drive character goals and story arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's Third Law (Focus on expanding existing elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Before adding something new to your system, first expand on what you already have.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer deepening and enriching existing mechanics or world elements over adding many new systems. Avoid bloat and compatibility problems (example: the D&D Mystic class becoming an overcomplicated 28‑page design). Expand existing features for depth and cohesion rather than proliferating new, poorly integrated mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hollow iceberg (design only what's necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of your world as an iceberg: the tip is explicitly defined worldbuilding; the rest is assumed or implied—only design what’s necessary for the game and its story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest time in a few deep, unique elements instead of many shallow ones (example: Skyrim’s many shallow dungeons). Hint at additional details to create the illusion of a deep world without exhaustive design. This conserves GM time and keeps player-facing content focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's Zeroth Law (Prioritize awesomeness / fun)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Always err on the side of what is awesome” — when in doubt, start with your most exciting idea and work backward to incorporate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let fun and interesting concepts guide design decisions. If a rule or world element that would be 'more correct' reduces player enjoyment, favor the option that creates memorable, exciting play—as long as it remains coherent with established rules or is retrofitted consistently.
